title: Beacon — architecture diagrams
subtitle: What is built today, and what the next phases add. Every diagram is generated from a source file in docs/diagrams/src.

groups.title: 1 · System structure
groups.blurb: Zooming in: who uses Beacon, which processes exist, what is inside them, and which module may import which.

groups.title: 2 · Data flow
groups.blurb: What data moves, where it rests, and where the trust boundaries are. Levels 0 → 2, in the usual DFD sense.

groups.title: 3 · Behaviour over time
groups.blurb: The three sequences that matter, plus the lifecycle of an item and of a signal.

groups.title: 4 · Data model
groups.blurb: The entities and tables, and the rule that nothing derived is ever stored.

groups.title: 5 · Running it
groups.blurb: Deployment today, what the logs already tell you, and the threats each control answers.

groups.title: 6 · Future phases (not built)
groups.blurb: Phase 4 (pilot) and phase 5 (enterprise). Purple, dashed boxes do not exist yet — that is the whole point of this section.

diagrams.title: System context (C4 level 1)
diagrams.summary: The one-page answer to "what is this thing and who touches it": three roles, Beacon in the middle, and three external systems.
diagrams.howToRead: Start with a person on the left and follow their arrow in, then follow what comes back out. Two arrows carry the product's whole stance: Beacon asks the AUTHOR to confirm before anyone else is told, and it writes back to the tracker only what a human approved.
review: Is any role missing an arrow it needs?
Is anything shown as an input that the system cannot actually see?

diagrams.title: Containers (C4 level 2)
diagrams.summary: The processes and stores that exist when Beacon is running: a browser, one Next.js server (UI + API + brain), the agent worker, and one of two stores.
diagrams.howToRead: Everything in the big box is one process — the brain is a library, not a service, which is why the browser and the server can never disagree about a score. The agent worker contains no logic at all: it is a clock that calls an endpoint.
review: Could the brain be imported by the browser and the server and still behave identically? (It must.)
Is the store choice visible to an operator at runtime? (/api/health says which one is live.)

diagrams.title: Inside the brain (C4 level 3)
diagrams.summary: The computation, in the order it happens: world → facts → detection → score → signals → questions and proposals.
diagrams.howToRead: Follow the arrows top to bottom; that is one run. The dashed arrow is the only way a model gets in — as a verdict for one exact piece of text, installed for the length of a run. Everything else is deterministic.
review: Does anything downstream of the score write back upstream? (It must not.)
Where would a new rule go, and would it show up in the reasons list automatically?

diagrams.title: Code map and import rules (C4 level 4)
diagrams.summary: Which module imports which, in three zones: the browser bundle, the shared brain, and server-only code.
diagrams.howToRead: The rule this diagram exists to enforce: nothing in the right-hand zone (lib/server, lib/llm, config) may ever be imported by a screen. If it were, a database URL or a model key would end up in the browser bundle.
review: Trace any screen to the right-hand zone — there should be no path.
Does the shared middle zone do any I/O? (It must not.)

diagrams.title: API surface and its guards
diagrams.summary: All ten endpoints (fourteen method-path pairs), grouped by what they can do: read, call a model, or change recorded state.
diagrams.howToRead: Read the guard box first — it applies to every route, which is why the route files themselves are four lines long. Then check the group a route sits in: that is the honest answer to "what can this endpoint do to me".
review: Is any route in the wrong group?
Should any read route also be rate limited?

diagrams.title: Data flow level 0 (context DFD)
diagrams.summary: Beacon as a single process, with every external entity and every labelled flow F1–F9 crossing the trust boundary.
diagrams.howToRead: The dashed box is the trust boundary. Flows that cross it are the ones a security or privacy review cares about — especially F8, the only flow that leaves infrastructure you control, and F7, the only flow that changes someone else's system.
review: Is F8 the minimum data that could possibly do the job?
Can F7 happen without a recorded human approval? (No — see diagram 13.)

diagrams.title: Data flow level 1 (processes and stores)
diagrams.summary: The nine numbered processes and four data stores, with every arrow labelled with what actually moves.
diagrams.howToRead: Follow 1 → 9 in order for a full cycle. Processes 7, 8 and 9 are red because they are the only ones that change stored state, and each has a human or a schedule behind it, never the agent on its own.
review: Does every arrow into a store have an identified actor?
Is there any path from process 6 (raise signals) directly to process 8 (write back)? There must not be — 7 sits between them.

diagrams.title: Data flow level 2 — the detector
diagrams.summary: Process 4 expanded: how a piece of update text becomes an explainable verdict, with or without a model.
diagrams.howToRead: The two boxes that carry the argument are "normalize" and "fall back to the rules". The model supplies phrases; the score is recomputed from them and the threshold is ours, so a model cannot assert a conclusion the evidence does not support.
review: If the provider returned a confident verdict with no phrases, what score would it get? (Zero.)
Is there any path where a model failure reaches the user as an error? (No — it degrades to rules.)

diagrams.title: How state is kept (base + decision log)
diagrams.summary: A read-only base snapshot plus an append-only log of human decisions, folded by one reducer that both the server and the browser run.
diagrams.howToRead: Note which event kinds are in the upper box: only two of the eight can change an item. The rest are recorded because they are evidence about the agent's usefulness, not because they change the board.
review: Could a signal decision silently change an item? (No.)
How is a mistake corrected? (A new event — event.undone — never by editing the log.)

diagrams.title: Privacy boundary — what leaves, what never does
diagrams.summary: Three columns: what stays in the viewer's browser, what stays in our store, and the short list that can leave for a model provider.
diagrams.howToRead: Read the "never sent" box as a specification, not a reassurance — it is what lib/llm/types.ts actually allows into a prompt. The default configuration sends nothing at all: with no key, the rule detector runs.
review: Does anything in "sent" identify a person beyond a first name?
If a customer forbids external model calls, what changes? (One environment variable.)

diagrams.title: Failure modes and graceful degradation
diagrams.summary: Every branch for "something is down", each ending in a state that still works and is visible to an operator.
diagrams.howToRead: Follow any "no" branch to its end: none of them reaches a dead end. The point is that the model and the database are both optional in different ways — the model is optional by design, the database is optional with a stated downgrade.
review: Which failures are silent? (None — each is logged or reported by /api/health.)
Is the file-store fallback ever chosen after Postgres has worked? (No — that would split the log.)

diagrams.title: Sequence — one scheduled agent run
diagrams.summary: The clock triggers a run; the server loads the world, reads each item's language, computes, and records one run row.
diagrams.howToRead: Check what is missing: there is no arrow to the tracker and no item change. A run reads, computes and records. The loop shows the model call and its fallback side by side.
review: What happens if a run takes longer than the interval? (Single flight — the next trigger joins it.)
Where does cost come from? (One model call per active item per run, which is why the route is rate limited.)

diagrams.title: Sequence — hidden blocker to approved change
diagrams.summary: The product's central claim as a single trace: detected wording → the author is asked first → a previewed proposal → an approval → the tracker.
diagrams.howToRead: Follow the happy path first, then the two alternatives. The "no" branch matters as much as the "yes": a dismissal is recorded with a reason, and a kind of signal that keeps being dismissed gets retuned rather than kept.
review: Is the author ever bypassed? (No.)
Is an approval reversible, and is the reversal visible? (Yes — event.undone.)

diagrams.title: Sequence — the one-field update composer
diagrams.summary: A person writes or dictates one note; the model tidies it or folds it with the thread; the person confirms every word before anything is posted.
diagrams.howToRead: Three nested fallbacks, each labelled with the `source` value the response carries: llm, rules, or rules-local. The UI shows which one produced the text, so the copy never claims a model ran when it did not.
review: Can the model post anything by itself? (No.)
With the static export and no backend, do both buttons still work? (Yes — rules-local.)

diagrams.title: State — the life of a work item
diagrams.summary: Every status an item can hold and every transition between them, with the scoring consequences of being blocked or overdue.
diagrams.howToRead: Each transition label names its cause, and every cause is a person. The two notes are the rules that make silence meaningful only where a daily update is actually expected.
review: Is there a transition the agent could make alone? (No.)
Are risks and decisions nagged for daily updates? (No — see the second note.)

diagrams.title: State — the life of a signal and its proposal
diagrams.summary: Open → accepted, dismissed or snoozed; and the nested lifecycle of the tracker change a signal proposes.
diagrams.howToRead: The nested box is a separate decision from the signal itself: you can accept that a problem is real and still reject the specific change proposed for it. The note explains how dismissals feed back into stated confidence.
review: Does a snoozed signal disappear? (No — the next run re-raises it.)
What stops the agent repeating a settled signal? (The decision is in the log, and the run reads it.)

diagrams.title: Journey — one day, by role
diagrams.summary: The same data through three lenses, as the sequence of things each role actually does in a day.
diagrams.howToRead: The scores are the intended experience for the person in that row, not a measurement. Read the manager section for what is deliberately absent: there is no per-person step anywhere in it.
review: Is any step in the member row more than one interaction? (It should not be.)
Does the manager row ever reach an individual's record? (No.)

diagrams.title: Data model today
diagrams.summary: The entities and their tables: a base snapshot of what the tracker gave us, the append-only decision log, and the run log.
diagrams.howToRead: Look for what is NOT a column: there is no attention score, no signal and no confidence anywhere. Those are computed on read, which is what makes "the score equals the sum of the reasons" enforceable.
review: Could any stored field drift out of agreement with a computed one?
Is anything in EVENT.payload that belongs in a column for querying?

diagrams.title: Deployment today — three ways to run it
diagrams.summary: The public static export, the full local/WSL stack, and the container stack — with what each one genuinely can and cannot do.
diagrams.howToRead: The red box in the first column is the honest part: the public URL has no API, so no shared log, no live agent and no model calls. The other two columns are the real system.
review: Is the limitation of the public demo visible to a visitor? (Yes — the privacy card names the live store.)
What is not automated yet? (The container image build.)

diagrams.title: Observability — how you find out something is wrong
diagrams.summary: What the system already emits (logs, run rows, health, adoption counters) and the phase-4 collection and alerting around it.
diagrams.howToRead: Left column is today; the purple middle is infrastructure a pilot adds. The right column is the useful part of this diagram: four alerts worth acting on, including one that is about the product being wrong rather than down.
review: Could an operator diagnose a failed update without shell access? (Yes — requestId in the response and the log.)
Is there a metric that would catch the agent being annoying rather than broken? (Dismissal rate.)

diagrams.title: Threat model — threat to control
diagrams.summary: Seven threat classes, each paired with the control that answers it and where that control lives in the code.
diagrams.howToRead: Read right to left to audit: for each control, ask whether it is in the code today. One row is purple — spoofing — because there is no authentication yet. That gap is stated here rather than papered over.
review: Is any control a document rather than code?
Which threat would you fix first for a pilot? (Spoofing — SSO plus server-side role checks.)

diagrams.title: Target architecture (phases 4–5)
diagrams.summary: What a pilot and then an enterprise deployment add: SSO, a sync service, a job queue, Redis, audit/export, and metrics.
diagrams.howToRead: Everything solid exists today and is not replaced; every purple dashed box is new. The shape of the argument is that the brain and the API survive unchanged — what grows around them is infrastructure.
review: Does anything purple require rewriting something solid?
Which purple box is required before two replicas can run? (Redis.)

diagrams.title: Data flow — two-way tracker sync (phase 4)
diagrams.summary: How tracker changes come in and approved changes go out: four mapped fields, an approval gate, an idempotent outbox, and an explicit conflict path.
diagrams.howToRead: Follow 1 → 9, then look at 10. The conflict branch is the design decision worth reviewing: when the tracker changed under us, Beacon re-raises it for a person instead of overwriting.
review: Is this a mirror? (No — four fields, deliberately.)
What stops a double write after a retry? (An idempotency key per change.)

diagrams.title: Sequence — webhook in, approved write out (phase 4)
diagrams.summary: A tracker edit triggers a scoped run; an approved change is written back only after re-checking that the issue has not moved.
diagrams.howToRead: Two guards carry this diagram: deduplication at the receiver (so a burst of edits is not a burst of model calls) and the cursor re-check before writing (so nothing is silently overwritten).
review: What happens to a conflict? (It goes back to the person with both versions.)
Is the write labelled in the tracker? (Yes — AI-assisted.)

diagrams.title: Deployment target (pilot and enterprise)
diagrams.summary: A single-tenant, single-region topology: ingress, two app replicas, a worker pool, managed Postgres, Redis, a secret manager, and observability.
diagrams.howToRead: The note at the bottom is the part that changes code rather than infrastructure: the rate limiter and the run lock are in-process today, so they must move to Redis before a second replica is honest.
review: What breaks first if you scale to two replicas without Redis?
Where does a data-residency customer diverge? (A self-hosted model.)

diagrams.title: Identity, roles and erasure (phase 4)
diagrams.summary: The model that replaces today's trusted `actor` string: tenants, users linked to an SSO subject, memberships, and an explicit permission set.
diagrams.howToRead: The two notes are the substance. The permissions list is what each role may do; the user note explains why erasure is pseudonymisation of the actor rather than deletion of events — and why it needs sign-in first.
review: Does the manager role hold any permission that could reach an individual?
After pseudonymisation, is the audit trail still complete? (Yes — the decision survives, the identity does not.)

diagrams.title: Data model additions (phases 4–5)
diagrams.summary: The new tables: tenancy and users, per-item sync state, an idempotent outbox, KB embeddings, and a daily snapshot row.
diagrams.howToRead: Compare with diagram 18: nothing existing changes shape, which is why this is additive rather than a migration. SNAPSHOT_DAY is the one that unlocks an honest burndown and cycle time — today's charts only draw the days they really have.
review: Is any new table duplicating something computable? (It should not be.)
Why store a daily snapshot at all? (A real burndown cannot be reconstructed from current state.)

diagrams.title: Roadmap — phases 1 to 5
diagrams.summary: What is done, what is in progress, and what a pilot would take. Dates for phases 1–3 are when the work happened.
diagrams.howToRead: Read the bar colours, not the calendar: phases 1–3 are complete, and the phase 4–5 bars are sized estimates for a pilot, not commitments. The hardening bar on 14 October is the work covered by docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md.
review: Is anything claimed as done that the tests do not cover?
Which phase-4 item unblocks the most others? (SSO and server-side roles.)
